media.narrative_summary: In this September 2026 video, creator Isaac Flath demonstrates Docling's new AFP print file reader introduced in version v2.128.0. He explains that AFP is used by IBM printing systems and that Docling now includes a specialized reader to extract text directly from these files. Testing on two public sample files, he shows the first produced searchable phrases like "C++ compiler" but also joined words and garbled characters, while the second came back mostly unreadable. He attributes the issues to an encoding limitation—the reader currently assumes only one encoding (cp500)—and notes Docling gives a warning about this. He also points out the scope limitation: AFP files can contain images and barcodes, but this MVP release only extracts text, which Docling explicitly states. Despite the limits, he concludes it is a useful start for getting searchable text out of legacy print files.

Testing on two public sample files, he shows the first produced searchable phrases like "C++ compiler" but also joined words and garbled characters, while the second came back mostly unreadable. He attributes the issues to an encoding limitation—the reader currently assumes only one encoding (cp500)—and notes Docling gives a warning about this. He also points out the scope limitation: AFP files can contain images and barcodes, but this MVP release only extracts text, which Docling explicitly states. media.narrative_summary: A presenter demonstrates Nutrient's new commercial 'Chart Parsing' model, which converts chart images into structured table data (JSON) by linking each value to its category and series. He references Nutrient's public benchmark showing the model outperforming general-purpose systems like Gemini 3.8 Flash and Claude Opus 5 at extracting data values. To test it, he uses a CDC bar chart titled 'Fruits' showing how often students eat fruit by race/ethnicity, noting the chart has no printed numbers above the bars. The model successfully identified the five population groups and five consumption frequency columns and estimated values — for example, returning 28.8% for the total population eating fruit less than once per day, compared to the correct 28.5% from the accompanying CDC report. He emphasizes the estimate was within about 0.3 percentage points, but cautions these are estimates, not exact values, and should be handled as such, especially in high-accuracy contexts like medicine. Overall, he praises the work on extracting chart values into data, noting many reports contain bar charts, pie charts, and scatter plots without individual labels, making automated extraction into tables, JSON, or CSV formats very helpful.
